summary: Describes a framework and requirements for a call processing language, a simple and standard way to implement and deploy Internet telephony services. Many services need elaborate signalling, so a shared language for describing them is useful. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of writing a big program every time you want your phone to do something clever, like forwarding calls, you write short simple instructions. This lays out what that language needs.

subtitle: A simple language for customizing how a phone network handles incoming calls.

tldr.problem: Internet telephony (SIP, H.323) lets users control their own phone services, but defining call handling rules is complex. A standard language for describing call routing and filtering would let users create services easily without writing full programs.
tldr.mechanism: CPL is a simple, non-Turing-complete language that lets users write scripts describing how an incoming call should be handled: forward it, reject it, log it, send it to voicemail, apply filters based on caller identity, time of day, or other conditions.
tldr.outcome: Users can deploy phone services without vendor involvement, and third parties can create and modify services for clients. The non-Turing-complete design ensures scripts always terminate and use bounded resources.

today: RFC 2824 is an Informational framework document describing requirements for call processing languages. The related RFC (reference [5] in the document, now RFC 3880) defines the actual CPL language syntax and semantics. CPL has been adopted by some VoIP providers and open-source SIP servers.

sections.title: Network-Based Services and User Control
sections.content:
In traditional telephone networks, services like call forwarding or call screening were created by telephone companies using proprietary tools. Internet telephony protocols like SIP and H.323 make it possible for end users and third parties to implement and deploy services themselves, without involving a service provider.

Some services work well on end devices (the user's phone or computer): call waiting, multi-party calls, and other features that depend on the specific device's state. But services involving user location, call distribution, or behavior when the user is unavailable must run in a network device (a proxy server, redirect server, or gatekeeper) that all calls pass through.

Call Processing Language (CPL) is a standard way for users to write simple scripts running in these network servers, describing how that server should handle incoming calls.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone can do some things itself: beep when another call comes in, mix three calls together. But finding where you are right now, or deciding 'if my boss calls, ring me immediately, otherwise send to voicemail' — the network needs to know those rules. CPL is how you tell it.

sections.title: CPL Architecture and Network Model
sections.content:
An Internet telephony network has two types of components. End systems (phones, computers, voicemail boxes) originate and receive calls and their media. Signalling servers (SIP proxies, SIP redirect servers, H.323 gatekeepers) route call setup messages and maintain user location databases. A CPL script replaces the basic location-database lookup in a signalling server, allowing complex logic instead of simple address translation.

A CPL script is associated with a particular user address (like sip:alice@example.com). When a call arrives at that server for that address, the script executes and decides: proxy the call to one or more other addresses, redirect the caller to a different address, or reject the call. Scripts run on servers the user trusts, and they may run on multiple servers along a call's path. The architecture does not require all servers to be controlled by the same organization.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of your address (your SIP name) as a mailbox. When someone tries to reach you, your script (your list of rules) runs at the mail center and decides 'deliver it to Alice's cell phone' or 'return to sender, she is busy.' Your script can run at your local post office, or at your company's mail center, or both.

sections.title: Simple, Safe Language Design
sections.content:
CPL deliberately avoids being Turing-complete. Rather than allowing arbitrary loops, recursion, or complex computation, it restricts itself to a simple condition-action model: if these conditions match, perform these actions. This design choice has several advantages. First, a script is guaranteed to terminate in bounded time and use bounded memory — the server cannot be attacked by an infinite loop or runaway computation. Second, scripts can be verified for correctness automatically: a tool can check whether the script contains unreachable code, contradictory conditions, or obvious errors. Third, scripts are easy for users to write, understand, and modify by hand or with tools.

This approach differs from using a general-purpose scripting language (Perl, Python, Tcl) or a full programming language sandboxed with resource limits. Without explicit resource limits in the language definition itself, a server never knows whether a particular script will run successfully on that server or on another.
sections.plainLanguage: A regular programming language can do almost anything: count forever, use gigabytes of memory, break in weird ways. CPL can only do specific phone-related things. It is like the difference between a general recipe book and a simple checklist: 'if it is dinner time, cook pasta; if it is breakfast time, make eggs.'

sections.title: Who Creates and Deploys Scripts
sections.content:
CPL scripts can be created and deployed in several ways. End users write simple scripts describing their own call handling preferences and upload them to a server. Third parties (service providers, consultants) create customized scripts for clients, deploying them on servers the client controls or the client's service provider controls. Administrators create system-wide scripts implementing policy or global functions, which may run alongside individual user scripts. Web middleware applications can generate CPL scripts on behalf of users through a graphical interface, hiding the language syntax from non-technical users.

Like HTML, which can be written by hand, generated by tools, or created by web servers, CPL scripts can be authored in multiple ways, and tools can create, edit, and understand scripts more easily than they could with a full programming language.
sections.plainLanguage: You can write your rules by hand if you are technical. A web tool can ask you 'where do you want calls to go?' and write the rules for you. Your company can have rules that apply to everyone. A consultant can set it up for you.

sections.title: Handling Feature Interactions and Ambiguity
sections.content:
Feature interaction — when two services produce conflicting or unexpected behavior — is a well-known problem in telephony. In traditional systems, users might subscribe to both 'call forwarding on busy' and 'call waiting,' creating ambiguity about what should happen when they are already on a call.

CPL reduces feature interaction through its explicit nature. A CPL script is a clear list of conditions and actions; when a user writes or approves it, they are explicitly deciding what to do in each situation. However, interactions can still occur in three scenarios: multiple scripts on the same server (a user's script and an administrative script, for example), scripts on different servers along a call path (the originator's server and the destination's server both have scripts), and server-to-server interactions (one script's action triggers another script). The RFC discusses how to order scripts correctly and acknowledges that server-to-server interactions are difficult to solve completely in a heterogeneous network.
sections.plainLanguage: If you say 'forward all calls to my cell phone' and 'reject all calls from strangers,' what happens when a stranger calls? CPL makes you decide this explicitly. But if your rule forwards a call, and the phone at the other end has a rule to forward it again, the phone system needs to be careful not to bounce it forever.

sections.title: Language Features and Requirements
sections.content:
A call processing language must support basic telephony operations: proxying calls to one or more addresses (with parallel ringing or sequential attempts), redirecting (returning alternate addresses to the caller), and rejecting calls. It must be able to make decisions based on the calling party's address, the destination address, time of day, user registration information, and other context. It must support logging for audit trails and may support sending notifications (e-mail, etc.) for administrative purposes.

The language should be lightweight and efficient, so it does not become a bottleneck on busy servers. It should be verifiable: before executing a script, the server should be able to detect obvious errors or contradictions. For security, scripts must be transported to servers with integrity protection (to prevent tampering), and only trusted users should be able to create scripts affecting a given address.
sections.plainLanguage: Your script needs to say things like 'if Alice calls, ring my office; if the time is after 5pm, ring my home; if I have 5 calls waiting, send the 6th to voicemail.' It should be fast, so the phone network does not slow down. And the phone network should be able to spot if your script is nonsense before it tries to run it.
